A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASAT and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-D. Retained experiments and material can be matched across renumbering and relocation, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original stationary and nonstationary OOD experiments, baseline comparisons, and analyses of window sizes and update frequencies.

after.justification: The original benchmark experiments are retained, and Appendix D.5 adds original simulations studying sensitivity to FPR tolerance, labeling probability, and OOD prevalence.

M1.justification: V2 introduces calibration-safe Algorithm 3: a newly trained scorer is calibrated exclusively on subsequent samples and deployed only when its threshold constraint becomes feasible, while the previous scorer remains active. This substantially changes calibration and deployment for the analyzed variant. Separately, the stated model-selection criterion changes from adding to subtracting twice the DKW margin in Section 3.2 and Appendix B.

E1.justification: V2 adds a synthetic Gaussian ID/OOD setting in Appendix D.5. The existing CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, and associated OOD coverage is retained. The MRI examples added to Figure 1 are illustrative, not an evaluated medical dataset.

E2.justification: The evaluated FSFT, FSAT, binary-classifier, and scoring-function comparisons are retained. Several names are corrected to match existing plots: for example, the ImageNet prose changes MSP/KNN to KNN/MDS, which were already the methods displayed in v1 Figure 15, now v2 Figure 14.

E3.justification: The new Gaussian study uses a linear scorer, 100,000 time steps, and separate sweeps of alpha, p, and gamma, reporting feasibility time and annotation counts alongside FPR/TPR. Existing benchmark settings are retained. V2 explicitly states that experiments use the practical algorithm, not the newly analyzed calibration-safe variant.

E4.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a targeted sensitivity analysis testing how FPR tolerance, labeling probability, and OOD prevalence affect safety, TPR, cold-start duration, and annotation cost. The existing window-size and update-frequency analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Existing experiments retain five repetitions with means and standard deviations. The new sensitivity table reports five seeds and uncertainty values, extending the existing repeated-run reporting practice without changing replication or uncertainty estimation for retained results.

E6.justification: The retained benchmark plots show unchanged results. New Table 4 adds simulation outcomes: at alpha=0.05 and p=gamma=0.2, reported FPR is 4.23 ± 0.21% and TPR is 87.41 ± 0.63%; increasing p from 0.05 to 0.40 increases mean human annotations from 36,235 to 59,535. These are newly reported results, not improvements over v1 under matched settings.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C substantially revise the guarantee and proof. Lemma 1 introduces the missing mixture factor gamma and E[Z]=gamma; Lemma 2 changes the martingale increments to Z times the centered indicator. Propositions 1-3 now use post-training calibration samples and conditioning on training history. Appendix D.2 also corrects its theoretical confidence-bound formula.

C1.justification: The central stationary FPR guarantee is narrowed from ASAT generally to the calibration-safe variant, with v2 explicitly stating that the experimental algorithm does not instantiate Proposition 1. The abstract also distinguishes stationary FPR control from transient violations during nonstationary adaptation. The central adaptive-scoring contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly separates empirical safety of the practical algorithm from the theoretical guarantee and identifies reuse of training samples for calibration as an unresolved theoretical issue in Appendix C, Remark 1. It also explains how distribution overlap limits TPR and interprets the new sensitivity results through annotation-cost and cold-start tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Appendix D.5 documents the new simulation's Gaussian means of 5.5 and -6, standard deviation of 4, linear scoring function, horizon, and exact parameter grids. Existing architecture descriptions, optimizer choices, and grid-search hyperparameters are retained.

R1.justification: Related work expands its discussion of scoring methods and adds comparison with Magesh et al. (2023) on multiple testing; the noise discussion adds Ibrahim et al. (2025). The DKW citation changes from Nadaraya (1965) to Dvoretzky et al. (1956), and the Ren/Kirichenko references disappear. The central positioning as online adaptation beyond fixed scoring remains.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much existing prose are retained, with targeted rewrites and substantial local expansion of related work. Algorithm 1 moves from Appendix B into the main text, an appendix contents list is added, title and author information are updated, and acknowledgments are removed.

P2.justification: V2 applies document-wide TMLR typography and front-matter formatting and rearranges displays. Figure 1 replaces digit/clothing illustrations with MRI examples, the former comparison Figure 2 becomes Table 1, and Algorithm 3 and the three-part sensitivity Table 4 are added. Existing performance plots are preserved, with several captions corrected.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is correction and qualification of the central safety argument: v2 repairs mixture-weighting and martingale errors and distinguishes the post-training calibration guarantee from heuristic experimental results. This addresses consequential mathematical and evidentiary weaknesses in v1. The sensitivity study and corrected captions add useful support and clarity. Although the analyzed variant remains unevaluated and some broad safety wording persists, the gain in mathematical accuracy and transparency is substantial.
